where: Section 3, paragraph starting 'Engine and APU bottles are usually fixed'
problem: It says engine extinguishing bottles are usually fixed in the nacelle. The nacelle is the fire zone itself: it is hot, vibrating and inaccessible, and the agent has to be delivered into it from outside. On jet transports the engine bottles sit in the fuselage or wing/fairing structure near the engine, with pipes running to the nacelle discharge nozzles. Only the APU bottle is in the tail cone/aft bay.
fix: Engine and APU bottles are fixed in the aircraft structure, not in the fire zone. The APU bottle sits in the tail cone or aft equipment bay; the engine bottles sit in the fuselage or wing root close to the engine, and pipes carry the agent to nozzles inside the nacelle.

problem: 'The bottle must hold 2.4 m³ of agent vapour' is misleading. The bottle stores the agent as a liquid under pressure; 2.4 m³ is the volume that vapour occupies after release and expansion in the zone.
fix: The released agent must occupy 2.4 m³ of the zone (as vapour at zone conditions), which needs 14.4 kg of agent stored in the bottle.

problem: This is an approximation that ignores the fact that the released agent displaces air in the zone. The standard total-flooding form divides by (1 − C), which matters when the concentration is not small.
fix: State the assumption, or give the standard form Va = C × Vz ÷ (1 − C), where Va is agent vapour volume in m³, C the design concentration as a fraction and Vz the zone volume in m³. For 6 % the two forms differ by about 6 %.

problem: The answer presents exactly four zones as the whole list. Many transport aircraft also have wheel-well fire detection and avionics/equipment-bay overheat or smoke detection, so a student may mark the four as universal.
fix: Ask for 'four zones protected on a typical transport aircraft' and answer 'engine, APU, cargo compartment and lavatory; many types also monitor the wheel well and the avionics bay'.

problem: The chapter never says that engine and APU detection loops are duplicated (an A loop and a B loop). This is why the control unit can show FIRE, FAULT or normal, and it is a standard exam point on how a single broken wire does not lose protection.
fix: Add: engine and APU zones usually have two identical loops. A fire on either loop gives a warning; a break in one loop gives a fault while the other loop still protects the zone.

where: Section 3, first paragraph after 'When the control unit confirms a fire'
problem: It implies an APU fire is always handled by the crew. On the ground, many types shut the APU down automatically and discharge the APU bottle without crew action; the crew handle is for in-flight use.
fix: Add: on the ground an APU fire normally trips an automatic APU shutdown and, on many types, an automatic bottle discharge; in flight the crew uses the APU fire handle.
